name: Chef studio tableware
summary: Hand-made stoneware plates and bowls that a studio potter makes with a chef for one restaurant. The pieces have an uneven rim, a matt or earth-toned glaze and a bare clay foot, and they frame the food like a landscape.

philosophy.core_thesis: A chef and a potter design the plate with the dish: a matt, earthy and slightly uneven vessel gives the food a ground that no factory plate can give.
design_principles: Throw each piece by hand on the wheel, and leave a trace of the throwing rings.
Make the rim a little uneven, and the well wide, so that the food sits like a landscape.
Glaze in a matt or ash glaze in an earth colour: stone, moss, rust, bone or charcoal.
Leave a bare clay foot and a bare patch where the piece stood in the kiln.
Make a new shape for each dish, in a run of 20 to 200 pieces.
Let the glaze move in the kiln: it pools, breaks at the edge and shows the body.
Fire in reduction at 1250 °C so that the iron shows in the glaze.
anti_patterns: A white factory plate with a gilt rim
A glossy, even and perfect glaze
A bright colour that competes with the food

form.shape: Wide, shallow plates with an uneven rim, deep bowls with a thick lip, slab platters, small tasting dishes and cups without a handle.
form.profile: A wide shallow well and a low, soft rim, or a deep bowl that curves up to a thick lip; the line is not exact.
form.foot_and_rim: A bare, turned foot ring with a rough ring of body; the rim is a soft, slightly uneven edge.
form.proportion: Plate diameter 20 to 32 cm, wall 4 to 8 mm thick; the well is wide and the rim is only about 15 per cent of the width.
rules: Keep the well wide, so that the food is the main shape.
Leave a small irregularity in the rim and the foot.
Make the piece for one dish, and test it with that dish.

bodies.rule: Use a stoneware with some grog or iron that shows through the glaze. Use porcelain for a fine small plate. Do not use factory bone china: the style is hand-made.

methods: mending with lacquer and gold, in the manner of kintsugi
forming.joins: A cup has no handle; a lid, when it is needed, fits a rebated seat that the potter checks by hand.
forming.details: Throwing rings on the wall, finger marks at the rim, a glaze that thins at the edge, and a stamp or a mark in the base.

glaze.pattern: No pattern; a bare band, a wax-resist ring, a fine incised line, or a glaze that runs in a soft pool.
glaze.gloss: Matt to satin, about 10 to 45 GU.
glaze.wear: The matt glaze shows cutlery marks, and the bare clay takes colour from food; makers regard this as part of the piece.

palette.strategy: Earth tones in a matt finish: stone, moss, rust, bone and charcoal, with one pale colour for contrast.

firing.kiln: A small gas or electric kiln, sometimes a wood or soda kiln, fired in reduction.
processes: glaze firing in reduction at about 1250 °C
sorting and numbering of the run
firing.scale: A studio of 1 to 10 people that makes runs of 20 to 200 pieces for one restaurant.
firing.signs: Throwing rings, a glaze that varies from piece to piece, a bare foot, and the stamp of the studio.

pieces.form: Wide shallow plate with an uneven rim and a matt stone glaze
Deep bowl with a thick lip, a throwing ring and an ash glaze that runs
Small porcelain plate with a satin glaze and a wax-resist ring
Slab platter with a bare clay edge and a shino glaze pool

positive: uneven soft rim and wide shallow well
matt earth-tone glaze, stone and moss
tasting menu dish on a dark table

canonical_works.maker: Heath Ceramics with Alice Waters and Christina Kim

canonical_works.work: Hand-thrown stoneware plates for New Nordic restaurants

emotion.target_response: A quiet, grounded attention: the viewer sees a plate that was made by hand for one dish, and looks at the food first.

avoid_when: the brief needs identical factory pieces
the brief wants gold or painted ornament
the brief wants bright gloss colour

modifiers.how: Make the shapes exact, stackable and in series, and keep the satin glaze and the plain surface.
Add a free brush stroke or a wax-resist pattern, and keep the stoneware body.
Change to a thin porcelain with a clear ivory glaze and a carved line.

sources.title: Vice: Meet the ceramicist turning plates into art for Copenhagen's best chefs
